title: Can You Fly With Weed? Michigan Travel Rules
h1: Flying With Cannabis From Michigan: The Rules Travelers Should Know
metaDescription: Can you fly with weed from Michigan? What TSA, federal and state rules mean for flower, edibles, vapes and CBD, and safer ways to plan around your trip.
excerpt: State-legal cannabis is still a federal problem at the airport. Here's what TSA does, how edibles, vapes and CBD fit in, and how to travel the legal way.
keyTakeaways: Airport screening and flights put you under federal law, where adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I as of October 2026.
TSA officers don't search for drugs, but they refer illegal substances they find to law enforcement.
Edibles, vapes and cartridges get no exemption, and a Michigan medical card doesn't change federal law.
Taking cannabis across a state line or an international border is illegal, even between two places where it's legal.
The legal plan: leave it at home, locked up, and buy at your destination only if it's legal there.
body:
Can you fly with weed? Not legally, even if you're flying between two legal states. Airport screening and air travel fall under federal law, and adult-use marijuana is still against federal law as of October 2026. Here's what TSA actually does, how edibles, vapes and CBD fit in, what medical patients should know and better ways to plan a trip from Michigan.

## Can you fly with weed? Federal law governs flights, even between legal states

Michigan's adult-use law lets anyone 21 or older carry as much as 2.5 ounces inside the state. That protection stops where federal law takes over. As of October 2026, marijuana stays in Schedule I of the federal Controlled Substances Act, with two narrow exceptions. Drug products the FDA has approved, and marijuana sold under a state medical marijuana license, moved to Schedule III. Anything sold for adult use is still Schedule I.

Carrying cannabis over a state line also remains illegal under federal law, even when the states on both sides have legalized it. At the airport, you're dealing with a federal agency from the moment you reach the checkpoint. For the bigger federal picture, see our [explainer on cannabis rescheduling](/blog/cannabis-rescheduling/).

## TSA's role: screening for safety, then referrals to police

TSA's job is security, and it says so plainly. Its officers don't search for illegal drugs. But if they discover an illegal substance or evidence of a crime during screening, TSA refers the matter to a law enforcement officer. The final decision on what goes through the checkpoint rests with the TSA officer.

TSA's medical marijuana entry marks carry-on and checked bags with special instructions, and the instruction it gives is that referral. It doesn't say you may fly with cannabis, and a police referral is the last thing you want on travel day.

## Michigan airports: what local authorities may do

Whether you're leaving from Detroit Metro, Grand Rapids or a regional airport, a TSA referral hands the decision to the officers who respond. No one can promise what they'll do. Michigan's protections cover adults 21 and older within the state's limits, but they don't make a flight legal, and federal law still applies. At the very least, a referral costs time, and it could cost you your flight.

Two more Michigan points apply at the airport:

- **No public use.** Public consumption is off-limits in Michigan, terminal and curbside included.
- **Under 21 isn't covered.** Michigan's adult-use law doesn't protect anyone under 21.

Our [Michigan cannabis law page](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) lays out the state's possession limits and penalties.

## Edibles, vapes and cartridges: no special exemption

Gummies, chocolates, drinks, vape cartridges and concentrates are cannabis too, so they sit in the same legal spot as flower. A product's form doesn't change its status, and neither does its packaging.

Vape devices raise one extra point. TSA allows [electronic smoking devices](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/items/electronic-cigarettes-and-vaping-devices) in carry-on bags only, never in checked bags, and sets limits on their lithium batteries. That's a battery-safety requirement, not a cannabis exemption: a cartridge filled with cannabis oil is still cannabis under federal law.

## Medical patients: a state card doesn't change federal law

A Michigan medical marijuana card protects registered patients under Michigan law. Federal law is a separate matter. As of October 2026, marijuana sold under a state medical license sits in federal Schedule III. The April 2026 federal rescheduling order that moved it there, though, is aimed at licensed medical businesses. Nothing in it says a patient can take medical cannabis over a state line or onto federal property, so those questions remain unresolved.

Until federal agencies say more, a card isn't a travel pass. If you're heading to another state, check whether it honors out-of-state cards. Our guide to [medical marijuana card reciprocity](/blog/medical-marijuana-card-reciprocity/) explains how that works, and your physician can help you plan for time away.

## Hemp-derived CBD: the 0.3% THC line and medicines approved by the FDA

Under current federal law, hemp is cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC, measured on a dry-weight basis, so many CBD products made from hemp fall outside the marijuana category. That line is moving. Congress has passed a narrower federal definition of hemp, set to take effect in late 2026 (as of October 2026; further changes are possible). It counts THCA toward the 0.3% limit and leaves out any finished hemp product with a container total above 0.4 mg of THC. Under the new rules, most intoxicating hemp-derived THC products would no longer count as hemp.

Medicines approved by the FDA are their own category. The same April 2026 order placed marijuana-containing drug products that the FDA has approved in Schedule III, and those aren't the same thing as anything sold in a dispensary. A product labeled CBD at a Michigan dispensary can contain enough THC to count as marijuana, so read our [hemp vs. marijuana guide](/blog/hemp-vs-marijuana-difference/) before you pack anything. When in doubt, leave it at home.

## International travel: serious penalties abroad

Crossing an international border with cannabis is riskier still. Canada, just across the river from Detroit, has legal cannabis. Even so, the Canadian government says it's illegal to take cannabis, including products containing cannabis, across the Canadian border in either direction unless Health Canada and the authorities of every country on your route have authorized it. Its travel advice adds that carrying any amount into another country, the United States included, can bring criminal charges, whether cannabis is legal there or not.

Farther afield, the stakes get higher. Canada's official travel advice warns that drug penalties abroad can include years or decades in a foreign prison, corporal punishment or even the death penalty. A U.S. state card or a Michigan receipt won't help you there. Check the laws at your destination and at any stopover before you go, and leave cannabis behind.

## Better plans: buy at your destination, leave it at home, store it safely

- **Buy at your destination if it's legal there.** Adults 21 and older visiting a state with legal adult-use sales can shop at a licensed store there. Follow that state's rules, and don't plan on bringing any of it home.
- **Leave it at home, locked up.** Store cannabis out of sight and out of reach while you're away, especially if anyone else will be in your home. Michigan already requires a lock on anything beyond 2.5 ounces kept at home.
- **Plan around the holidays.** Visiting family, or hosting once you're back? Our [holiday party guide](/blog/cannabis-holiday-party-guide/) covers etiquette for gatherings where cannabis is legal and welcome.

## Driving instead: crossing into Indiana and other states

Driving doesn't solve the problem. Federal law still forbids taking cannabis over a state line by car, and neighboring states add their own rules:

- **Indiana** allows neither adult-use nor medical marijuana, and Michigan-bought cannabis is just as illegal there as any other. Possession there counts as a Class B misdemeanor; the penalty can reach 180 days behind bars and a fine of as much as $1,000, and the charge climbs for people with prior drug convictions.
- **Illinois** lets adults 21 and older buy and possess cannabis, but [Illinois's own guidance](https://cannabis.illinois.gov/about/faqs.html) warns against moving cannabis across state lines.
- **Ohio and Wisconsin** sit across a state line too, so the same federal law applies.

Visiting our [New Buffalo store](/dispensary-locations/new-buffalo/) from Indiana or Chicago? Keep your purchase on the Michigan side, and don't travel across state lines with cannabis. Within Michigan, never use cannabis while driving. The cautious way to carry it is sealed, in the trunk or somewhere out of reach.

21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Can you fly with weed within Michigan?
faq.a: Not legally. Even a flight that never leaves Michigan starts at a TSA checkpoint, and TSA refers illegal substances it finds to law enforcement. Federal law, under which adult-use marijuana is still Schedule I as of October 2026, applies at the airport and in the air. Michigan's protections for adults 21+ don't override federal law.

faq.q: Will TSA arrest you for weed?
faq.a: TSA's role is security screening, not drug enforcement, and its officers don't search for drugs. If they find an illegal substance during screening, though, they refer the matter to a law enforcement officer, who decides what happens next. That can mean questions, a delay or a missed flight, so the safest plan is to leave cannabis at home.

faq.q: Can you bring edibles on a plane?
faq.a: Not legally. Gummies, chocolates and drinks containing THC are cannabis under federal law, the same as flower, and TSA refers illegal substances it finds to law enforcement. Packaging doesn't change that. If you're visiting a state with legal sales and you're 21 or older, buy there instead, and don't bring any home.

faq.q: Can you fly with a vape pen?
faq.a: A vape device itself follows TSA's rules for electronic smoking devices: carry-on bags only, never checked bags, with limits on lithium batteries. A cannabis cartridge is a different matter. It's still cannabis under federal law, with no exemption for the format, so leave cannabis vapes and cartridges at home.

faq.q: Can medical patients fly with cannabis?
faq.a: A Michigan card doesn't make it legal. As of October 2026, marijuana sold under a state medical license sits in federal Schedule III. But that change is aimed at licensed businesses, and it doesn't say patients may carry cannabis across state lines or onto federal property. Check whether your destination honors out-of-state cards, and plan with your physician before you travel.
